html:
A horse-drawn machine for cutting grain, shown in Virginia in 1831 by Cyrus McCormick and patented in 1834. Others had tried such machines; McCormick built on his father's work, with help from Jo Anderson, a man enslaved on the family farm.

A cutting bar with a moving blade sliced the stalks, a turning reel pushed them back, and they fell onto a platform to be raked off. With it a few people could harvest as much wheat in a day as a large gang with hand tools.

McCormick moved to Chicago in 1847 to be near the prairie wheat lands, and he sold on credit with guarantees. The reaper won a prize at the Great Exhibition in London in 1851. In the Civil War machines let Northern farms keep harvesting while men were away fighting.

The machine was part of the wider mechanisation of farming that pushed people off the land and into cities. In 1886 a strike at the McCormick works helped lead to the Haymarket affair.
